metadata.title: O'Dell v. Netherland, 521 U.S. 151 (1997) (No. 96-6867)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: O'Dell v. Netherland

Opinion filed: 1997-06-19

Docket No.: 96-6867

Citations:
• 138 L. Ed. 2d 351
• 117 S. Ct. 1969
• 521 U.S. 151
• 1997 U.S. LEXIS 3862

Case holding summaries:
• conviction became final upon denial of certiorari to state's highest court
• holding that Simmons announced a new rule of law for which habeas corpus relief is not available retroactively
• holding that Simmons announced a new rule and retrospective application of the rule was barred by Teague
• discussing Simmons v. South Carolina, 512 U.S. 154, 114 S.Ct. 2187, 129 L.Ed.2d 133 (1994) (plurality opinion), and finding that " Simmons is an unlikely candidate for `old-rule' status. As noted above, there was no opinion for the Court."
• recognizing Justice White's view as the rule of Gardner
• finding support for its conclusion that a case announced a new rule "in the decisions of the state courts and the lower federal courts," none of which previously had adopted the rule
• explaining that the Teague doctrine applies when a state prisoner seeks to overturn his conviction or sentence on federal collateral review
• noting that "the unique character of the death penalty mandates special scrutiny" of trial and sentencing procedures in capital cases
• "[W]henever a procedural rule is derived from state statutes and supreme court rules ... the rule is necessarily `firmly established.'"
• holding that "narrow right of rebuttal" established by Simmons v. South Carolina, 512 U. S. 154 (1994), "has hardly alter[ed] our understanding of the bedrock procedural elements essential to the fairness of a proceeding" (internal quotation marks omitted; emphasis in original)
• holding that the rule in Simmons v. South Carolina, 512 U. S. 154 (1994), which has been described as serving "one of the hallmarks of due process," id., at 175 (O'Connor, J., concurring in judgment), did not fit within the second Teague exception
• citing, as evidence that Caldwell v. Mississippi, 472 U. S. 320 (1985), announced a new rule, the views of the three Caldwell dissenters
• asserting that consideration by a capital sentencing jury of a defendant's prospects for commutation or parole is unconstitutional
• "A holding constitutes a `new rule' within the meaning of Teague if it `breaks new ground,' `imposes a new obligation on the States or the Federal Government,' or was not ` dictated by precedent existing at the time the defendant's conviction became final' "
• listing the States whose capital punishment schemes in one way or another require the jury to be informed that life without parole is either the only available alternative sentence or one of the options from which the jury is free to choose
• holding that the rule announced in Simmons v. South Carolina, 512 U.S. 154, 114 S.Ct. 2187, 129 L.Ed.2d 133 (1994
• holding that the Simmons rule does not constitute an exception to the ordinary non-retroactivity of new constitutional rules under Teague
• holding a "new rule" either "breaks new ground," "imposes a new obligation on the States or the Federal Government," or was not "dictated by precedent existing at the time the defendant's conviction became final"
• same, and noting a “new” constitutional rule is one that would have made a court considering a defendant’s direct appeal feel “compelled by existing precedent to conclude that the rule [he] seeks was required by the Constitution” (internal citations and quotations marks omitted)
• explaining that the Teague doctrine applies when a prisoner seeks to overturn his state conviction or sentence
• "Petitioner's conviction became final on October 3, 1988, when we declined to review the Virginia Supreme Court's decision affirming his sentence on direct review."
• holding that Simmons rule was a new rule that could not be used to disturb habeas petitioner's death sentence
• holding the requirement to inform juries that a defendant was not eligible for parole if the prosecution argues future dangerousness was a new rule under Teague v. Lane, 489 U.S. 288, 109 S.Ct. 1060, 103 L.Ed.2d 334 (1989)
• utilizing Marks analysis to discern a holding in Gardner v. Florida, 430 U.S. 349 (1977)
• declaring that Simmons announced a "new rule" under Teague for all already final convictions
• "[W]e will not disturb a final state conviction or sentence unless it can be said that a state court, at the time the conviction or sentence became final, would have acted objectively unreasonably by not extending the relief later sought in federal court."
• holding that a "new rule" either "breaks new ground," "imposes a new obligation on the States or the Federal Government," or was not "dictated by precedent existing at the time the defendant's conviction became final"
• "Teague asks state court judges to judge reasonably, not presciently."
• "The decision whether or not to inform the jury of the possibility of early release is generally left to the States."
• holding a "new rule" either "breaks new ground," "imposes a new obligation on the States or the Federal Government," or was not "dictated by precedent existing at the time the defendant's conviction became final"
• "[t]he array of views expressed in Simmons [v. South Carolina, 512 U.S. 154 (1994)] itself suggests that the rule announced there was, in light of this Court's precedent, susceptible to debate among reasonable minds" (internal quotation marks and citations omitted)
• explaining that the Teague doctrine applies when a prisoner seeks to overturn his state conviction or sentence
• Simmons is a "new rule" under the Teague doctrine
• explaining that the Teague doctrine applies when a state prisoner seeks to overturn his conviction or sentence on federal collateral review
• right of rebuttal afforded to defendants in a “limited class of capital cases” was not as “sweeping” as Gideon
• holding that the rule in Simmons v. South Carolina, 512 U.S. 154, 114 S.Ct. 2187, 129 L.Ed.2d 133 (1994
• noting that new rules are to be applied retroac‐ tively where they “forbid[] criminal punishment of certain primary con‐ duct” (internal quotation marks omitted)
• "Before a state prisoner may upset his state conviction or sentence on federal collateral review, he must demonstrate as a threshold matter that the court-made rule of which he seeks the benefit is not `new.'"
• adopting opinion from Gardner v. Florida, 430 U.S. 349 (1977), that predicts majority result even when Justices in prior precedent had based reasoning on different constitutional amendments
• adopting controlling opinion from Gardner v. Florida, 430 U.S. 349 (1977), despite the fact that plurality and concurrences based reasoning on different 11 constitutional amendments
• " Teague asks state-court judges to judge reasonably, not presciently."
• "[W]e will not disturb a final state conviction or sentence unless it can be said that a state court, at the time the conviction or sentence became final, would have acted objectively unreasonably by not extending the relief later sought in federal court."
• holding that extending the rule of Simmons would establish a new rule of constitutional law not within one of the exceptions to Teague v. Lane, 489 U.S. 288, 109 S.Ct. 1060, 103 L.Ed.2d 334 (1989
• holding that extending the rule of Simmons would establish a new rule of constitutional law not within one of the exceptions to Teague v. Lane, 489 U.S. 288, 109 S.Ct. 1060, 103 L.Ed.2d 334 (1989), and therefore inapplicable retroactively on collateral review
• rule requiring capital defendant to be allowed to inform sentencing jury of parole eligibility is a new rule
• same holding regarding the rule of Simmons v. South Carolina, 512 U.S. 154, 114 S.Ct. 2187, 129 L.Ed.2d 133 (1994)
• defendant's right to advise capital sentencing jury about parole eligibility not watershed rule
• "Petitioner's conviction became final on October 3, 1988 when we declined to review the Virginia Supreme Court's decision affirming his sentence on direct review."
